explanations.explanation: Wrath is it, baker. John says the angels hold the seven final plagues, “…with which the wrath of God is completed.” (Revelation 15:1) Seven plagues, and then it's finished. Not one more batch sitting in the back of the oven.

Harvest has a fair claim, baker, since John saw a sickle swung over the earth just before this (Revelation 14:16). Here, though, the verse says the seven final plagues are the ones “…with which the wrath of God is completed.” (Revelation 15:1) Wrath is the word that fills this blank.

The temple does show up in this passage, friend, and it gets very busy. But the blank isn't about a place. Revelation 15:1 says these final plagues are the ones with which “…the wrath of God is completed.” The word is wrath.

True! John says they were “…holding harps from God…” (Revelation 15:2) These are the ones who conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name, and they're standing beside something like a sea of glass mixed with fire. Harps in hand, ready to sing.

This one's true, friend. John says the people standing beside something like a sea of glass “…were holding harps from God…” (Revelation 15:2) They had conquered the beast and its image and the number of its name. And right after the harps comes the singing.

Moses it is. Moses was Israel's leader, and the singers sing “…the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb…” (Revelation 15:3) Moses and the Israelites once sang a song to the LORD too (Exodus 15:1). Two names on one song, and John gives us both.

David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), is a fair guess with all those harps around. But John never names him here. The song is called “…the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb…” (Revelation 15:3) The other name is Moses.

Elijah, the prophet who faced Israel's king Ahab (1 Kings 18:17-18), is a big name, friend. But he isn't in this verse. John says they sang “…the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb…” (Revelation 15:3) The other name is Moses.
That's the reason they give. They sing, “Who will not fear You, O Lord, and glorify Your name? For You alone are holy.” (Revelation 15:4) Notice the word alone. They aren't comparing Him to anybody.

explanations.answer: Because the sea obeys His voice
explanations.explanation: The singers are standing beside something like a sea of glass, so I see how that one sneaks in. But the song never says a sea obeys Him. Their reason is, “For You alone are holy.” (Revelation 15:4)

Plenty of angels in this passage, baker, but nobody sings about their sleep schedule. The song asks, “Who will not fear You, O Lord, and glorify Your name?” and then gives the reason: “For You alone are holy.” (Revelation 15:4) Sleep never comes up in it.

The song says the opposite. It says, “All nations will come and worship before You, for Your righteous acts have been revealed.” (Revelation 15:4) All nations, friend, not a few. Easy to miss when you're reading fast.
False is right. The song says, “All nations will come and worship before You, for Your righteous acts have been revealed.” (Revelation 15:4) Not a few nations. All of them.

Bowls, baker. One of the four living creatures gave the angels “…seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives forever and ever.” (Revelation 15:7) Golden bowls, and every one of them full. Keep an eye on those bowls, because the angels get their orders in the next chapter.

Trumpets do play a big part earlier in Revelation (Revelation 8:6), so I understand the guess. But in this passage the creature hands over “…seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God…” (Revelation 15:7) Bowls are what get poured out in chapter 16.

Crowns are a good guess, since Revelation has elders wearing golden crowns (Revelation 4:4). Here, though, the living creature gives the angels “…seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God…” (Revelation 15:7) Bowls, not crowns.

Not yet, friend. John says, “…no one could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.” (Revelation 15:8) The temple is filled with smoke from the glory of God and from His power, and nobody goes in until the plagues are done.

False is right. The temple is filled with smoke from God's glory and His power, and “…no one could enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were completed.” (Revelation 15:8) Nobody walks in until the plagues are done.

explanations.answer: Those with the mark of the beast
explanations.explanation: Right. The sores break out “…on those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.” (Revelation 16:2) The text names exactly who gets them. The passage keeps being that specific, so keep reading carefully.

The bowl is poured on the earth, so that's an understandable guess. But the text is more specific. The sores break out “…on those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.” (Revelation 16:2)

explanations.answer: Those beside the sea of glass
explanations.explanation: Those folks are standing beside something like a sea of glass, holding harps and singing (Revelation 15:2-3), so they're in a very different spot. They're the ones who conquered the beast and its image. The sores go to “…those who had the mark of the beast and worshiped its image.” (Revelation 16:2)
Dies. The sea turns to blood “…like that of the dead, and every living thing in the sea died.” (Revelation 16:3) This is a heavy one, friend. The text says every living thing.

Fleeing would mean they got away, baker, and the text doesn't say that. It says the sea turned to blood “…like that of the dead, and every living thing in the sea died.” (Revelation 16:3) It's a heavy verse.
Hiding would mean they had somewhere to go. Revelation 16:3 says the sea turned to blood “…like that of the dead, and every living thing in the sea died.” This part is heavy.

explanations.answer: They spilled the blood of saints and prophets
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the angel gives. He says, “For they have spilled the blood of saints and prophets, and You have given them blood to drink, as they deserve.” (Revelation 16:6) I think this one hurts to read. But the angel of the waters states the reason right there.

explanations.answer: They poisoned the rivers and springs
explanations.explanation: The rivers and springs turned to blood, so I see where that comes from. But the angel never says the people poisoned them. His reason is, “For they have spilled the blood of saints and prophets…” (Revelation 16:6)

explanations.answer: They tore down the temple of God
explanations.explanation: The temple is all over this passage, friend, so it's a natural guess. But the angel of the waters doesn't mention it as his reason. He says, “For they have spilled the blood of saints and prophets…” (Revelation 16:6)

True! John hears the altar reply, “Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are Your judgments.” (Revelation 16:7) The angel of the waters speaks first, then the altar answers. Two voices, and they agree about God's judgments.
This one's true, baker. John says, “And I heard the altar reply: ‘Yes, Lord God Almighty, true and just are Your judgments.’” (Revelation 16:7) The altar agrees with the angel of the waters.

Not this time, friend. The people were scorched by intense heat, “…and they cursed the name of God, who had authority over these plagues.” (Revelation 16:9) The text adds, “Yet they did not repent and give Him glory.”
False is right. John says they “…cursed the name of God, who had authority over these plagues. Yet they did not repent and give Him glory.” (Revelation 16:9) The heat came, and repenting did not.

explanations.answer: They curse the God of heaven
explanations.explanation: That's what the text says. The men “…curse the God of heaven for their pains and sores. Yet they did not repent of their deeds.” (Revelation 16:11) I think this is a hard verse to read.

I wish the text went that way, baker, but it doesn't. Instead the men “…curse the God of heaven for their pains and sores.” (Revelation 16:11) The verse adds, “Yet they did not repent of their deeds.”

The bowl goes on the throne of the beast, and its kingdom is plunged into darkness, so I see why that came to mind. But the text never says they turn on the beast. It says they “…curse the God of heaven for their pains and sores.” (Revelation 16:11)

explanations.answer: To prepare the way for the kings of the East
explanations.explanation: Yes, that's the reason given, baker. The sixth angel's bowl goes on the Euphrates, “…and its water was dried up to prepare the way for the kings of the East.” (Revelation 16:12) The purpose comes in the same sentence as the drying, so no guessing needed.

explanations.answer: To let God's people cross over safely
explanations.explanation: A river drying up so people can cross sounds like a story you might have heard before. But this verse doesn't say that. It says the water “…was dried up to prepare the way for the kings of the East.” (Revelation 16:12)

explanations.answer: To end the plague of blood in the rivers
explanations.explanation: The rivers did turn to blood back in verse 4, so I get the link. But the text doesn't connect the two. The Euphrates dries up “…to prepare the way for the kings of the East.” (Revelation 16:12)

Battle, baker. The spirits go out to the kings of the earth “…to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.” (Revelation 16:14) These are demonic spirits, and they perform signs as they go. I think a sign is how you get a whole crowd of kings to show up for something.

Worship is a good word, and the beast's image does get worshiped earlier in this passage (Revelation 16:2). But here the spirits go out “…to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.” (Revelation 16:14) So the blank wants battle.
A big crowd of kings could be for a lot of things, friend. But Revelation 16:14 says the spirits go out “…to assemble them for battle on the great day of God the Almighty.” Battle is the word.

True. Right after “Behold, I am coming like a thief.” the verse says, “Blessed is the one who remains awake and clothed, so that he will not go naked and let his shame be exposed.” (Revelation 16:15) The blessing goes to the one who stays awake and clothed. A blessing in the middle of all those bowls.

This one's true, baker. After “Behold, I am coming like a thief.” comes, “Blessed is the one who remains awake and clothed…” (Revelation 16:15) It's one verse, and the blessing comes right behind the warning.
“It is done!” That's the loud voice from the throne in the temple. (Revelation 16:17) It comes when the seventh angel pours out his bowl into the air. Seven bowls, seven angels, and then those words.

No second round here, friend. The seventh angel pours out his bowl into the air, and the voice from the throne says, “It is done!” (Revelation 16:17) That's the last of the seven, and the voice doesn't send anyone back to pour.

The temple was opened back in Revelation 15:5, so I see where that came from. But after the seventh bowl, the voice from the throne says, “It is done!” (Revelation 16:17) The voice says nothing about opening anything.

explanations.answer: Greatest since people came on the earth
explanations.explanation: That's what John says. He lists lightning, rumblings, thunder and “…a great earthquake the likes of which had not occurred since men were upon the earth—so mighty was the great quake.” (Revelation 16:18) Nothing like it had happened since people were on the earth.

explanations.answer: Strong enough to shake only the great city
explanations.explanation: The great city does get hit hard, and it splits into three parts. But the text says the quake is “…the likes of which had not occurred since men were upon the earth…” (Revelation 16:18) That's far bigger than one city.

explanations.answer: Mighty but over in a single moment
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give us a time on this quake, baker, so a single moment is an addition. What it does say is that it was “…a great earthquake the likes of which had not occurred since men were upon the earth…” (Revelation 16:18) That's the part to hold on to.

Collapse. The great city was split into three parts, “…and the cities of the nations collapsed.” (Revelation 16:19) The quake doesn't stop at one city. The text says the cities of the nations, plural.

Rejoice is a hopeful word, friend, but this verse doesn't mention any celebrating. The text says the great city was split into three parts, “…and the cities of the nations collapsed.” (Revelation 16:19) Collapsed is what fills the blank.

Nothing about rebuilding shows up in this verse, baker. It says the great city was split into three parts, “…and the cities of the nations collapsed.” (Revelation 16:19) Collapse is the word that fits.

True. The verse says, “And God remembered Babylon the great and gave her the cup of the wine of the fury of His wrath.” (Revelation 16:19) God is the one who remembers her and the one who gives her the cup. Nobody else hands it over, and nobody has to hold the door for it either.
This one's true, baker. Revelation 16:19 says God “…remembered Babylon the great and gave her the cup of the wine of the fury of His wrath.” Babylon the great is the one who gets the cup.

True. The verse says, “And men cursed God for the plague of hail, because it was so horrendous.” (Revelation 16:21) Hailstones of almost a hundred pounds each rain down, and men curse God for that plague. Earlier, people also cursed His name (Revelation 16:9). It's a heavy way to end the bowls.

This one's true, friend. The text says, “And men cursed God for the plague of hail, because it was so horrendous.” (Revelation 16:21) The hailstones weighed almost a hundred pounds each, and cursing is what the men did.
